meta.label: Fall Town Meeting
notes: One session, 14 articles. Monday, November 9 at 7:00 PM in the Medway High School Auditorium, 88 Summer Street. Warrant signed by the Select Board on October 23, 2026.
Free Cash is the big money story. Articles 2–5 move about $4.27M out of Certified Free Cash — $4.0M of it into the Capital Stabilization Fund (Art. 2).

Two citizens' petitions on license plate readers (Arts. 12–13). The Select Board recommends Disapprove on both; the Finance Committee takes No Position on Art. 12 and recommends Disapprove on Art. 13.
Finance Committee recommendation still open on Art. 14 ($1.04M raised on the tax levy for debt service and revaluation) — listed as To Be Determined in the warrant.
Higher vote thresholds. Four zoning articles (9, 10, 11, 13) generally need a two-thirds vote. Paying prior-year bills (Art. 1) needs nine-tenths at a meeting other than the Annual Town Meeting.

articles.title: Free Cash Transfer to Capital Stabilization Fund
articles.summary: Moves $4,000,000 of Certified Free Cash into the Capital Stabilization Fund, a reserve for future capital needs. By far the largest dollar item on the warrant. Town officials have tied it to future debt for the proposed Municipal Complex, which is expected to be voted on in spring 2027.
questions: If FY27 Free Cash is about $7.7M, what is planned for the roughly $3.4M not used on this warrant?
How much of the Municipal Complex's future debt is this reserve expected to cover, and over how many years?
What will the Capital Stabilization Fund balance be after this transfer?
If the Municipal Complex is not approved in spring 2027, what would this money be used for?
articles.text: To see if the Town will vote to transfer $4,000,000 from Certified Free Cash to the Capital Stabilization Fund, or act in any manner relating thereto.

background.html:
In short: According to the Town Manager, this $4M transfer is meant to build up reserves to help pay future debt on the proposed Municipal Complex, the major municipal facilities project whose construction funding is expected to be voted on in spring 2027. Article 2 does not approve that project. It moves money into a reserve, and spending from a stabilization fund takes a separate two-thirds Town Meeting vote.

What the money is for

In his report to the Select Board on October 5, the Town Manager described the Fall Town Meeting Free Cash transfers as intended to offset future debt payments for the major municipal facilities project, while also addressing rising vehicle and equipment replacement costs.

Where it comes from

  • The Town Manager put FY27 Certified Free Cash at about $7.7 million. The minutes call this a "projection."
  • Articles 2–5 on this warrant use about $4.27M of it ($4.0M of which is Article 2), which would leave roughly $3.4M if the $7.7M figure holds.

How it connects to the Municipal Complex

  • Funding to build the Municipal Complex is expected to be voted on in spring 2027.
  • According to the minutes, the financing strategy relies heavily on the $3 million PILOT agreement with the Medway Energy Center, the battery storage facility approved at the May 2026 Annual Town Meeting.
  • On October 5 the Select Board approved construction-phase contracts for the project's owner's project manager (Colliers, $1,548,767) and designer (Dore + Whittier, $2,439,400). Both take effect only if voters approve the project. The minutes also refer to $7.9M previously appropriated at Town Meeting and a "revisited borrowing amount of $6.9 million."
  • A public forum was scheduled for October 29 at the Thayer Homestead, where the project architects were to present designs, neighborhood impact mitigations and phased financing options.
A discrepancy in the minutes: The draft October 5 minutes say "$4,167,000 is going into the facility stabilization fund." The approved minutes instead say "$1 million will go into the general stabilization fund." The warrant itself, which is what Town Meeting votes on, says $4,000,000 to the Capital Stabilization Fund (Art. 2) and $100,000 to the General Stabilization Fund (Art. 3).
Sources:
  • Select Board minutes, Oct 5, 2026 (Town Manager's Report; Municipal Complex contracts) · packet
  • Select Board packet, Oct 19, 2026 (includes draft Oct 5 minutes and draft warrant)
  • Select Board minutes, Sep 21, 2026 (warrant closed)
  • All meetings: Select Board · Finance Committee (Oct 14 and Oct 20 agendas include warrant review and votes; minutes not yet posted)

articles.title: Sewer Retained Earnings: Purchase of Sewer Capacity from Franklin
articles.summary: Spends $1,075,000 of sewer enterprise savings (not tax money) toward a $1,575,000 purchase of 150,000 gallons per day of wastewater capacity from Franklin at the Charles River Pollution Control District plant. $800,000 of it is to be reimbursed by the Heritage on Main developer. Authorizes the Select Board and Town Manager to sign the agreements.
questions: Has the Planning Board approved Heritage on Main, and is the $800,000 reimbursement a binding commitment? What happens if the project does not go ahead?
Does owning more capacity raise Medway’s yearly operating costs at the treatment plant?
What happens to Medway’s purchase if Millis’s Town Meeting does not fund its share?
Which developments, beyond Heritage on Main, are expected to use the added capacity?
How much capacity is currently lost to groundwater leaking into the pipes, and how does the repair program affect the need for more?
articles.text: To see if the Town will vote to transfer $1,075,000 from Certified Sewer Enterprise Fund Retained Earnings for the purpose of purchasing 150,000 gallons-per-day of sewer capacity from the Town of Franklin pursuant to agreements with the Town of Franklin and the Charles River Pollution Control District, and further to authorize the Select Board and the Town Manager to take any action and execute any documents or agreements necessary to effectuate the purposes of this article, or act in any manner relating thereto.
articles.share_note: Paid from sewer enterprise retained earnings rather than general Town funds.

background.html:
In short: The full purchase is $1,575,000 for 150,000 gallons per day of capacity at the Charles River Pollution Control District plant. Article 6 covers the $1,075,000 coming from sewer savings; the rest comes from a development-agreement account. The Select Board approved the purchase 5–0 on September 8, and the agreement with Franklin is signed. It needs this Town Meeting vote for funding.

The deal

  • Medway, Millis and Franklin negotiated for years over Franklin’s excess capacity at the shared treatment plant. The price came down from $15.07 to $10.50 per gallon; 150,000 gallons per day × $10.50 = $1,575,000.
  • The purchase brings Medway’s total capacity to just over 1.1 million gallons per day.
  • The Board hired special counsel (Chris Petrini) for the negotiation.

How it’s paid for

  • $500,000 from a special revenue account funded by the 39 Main Street development agreement.
  • $1,075,000 from sewer enterprise retained earnings (this article), of which $800,000 is to be reimbursed by the Heritage on Main developer when it pulls building and occupancy permits.
  • If that reimbursement comes through, sewer savings net out at about $275,000.

Why now

On September 8 a Board member said Medway currently has about 80,000 gallons per day of unused capacity and described the purchase as proactive, for the town’s growth rather than immediate needs. Officials called it a 20-to-40-year solution that avoids major sewer rate increases.

In July the Board also discussed “the current sewer capacity issue,” which DPW tied partly to groundwater leaking into manholes and trunk lines. A separate contract to find and repair leaks ($78,720) is funded from a sewer repair account of about $400,000.

Still open

  • The plant’s three-town district agreement needs an amendment to reflect the new capacity numbers; counsel is drafting it.
  • Millis must also approve its share at its own Town Meeting.
  • As of late July, Heritage on Main still needed Planning Board approval. The $800,000 reimbursement depends on that project going ahead.
Sources:
  • Select Board minutes, Sep 8, 2026 (purchase approved; price and capacity) · packet (includes draft Jul 28 and Aug 10 minutes)
  • Select Board minutes, Sep 21, 2026 (funding breakdown)
  • Select Board minutes, Oct 5, 2026 (status; Millis)
  • All meetings: Select Board
Summary prepared with AI assistance from posted Select Board minutes and packets. The minutes paraphrase the discussion; the purchase agreement itself was not in the posted materials.

articles.title: Zoning: Nonconforming Uses and Structures
articles.summary: Updates Section 5.5 to match recent changes to the state Zoning Act (G.L. c. 40A). Key effects: permits stay protected from later zoning changes for 24 months instead of 12; homes that are nonconforming only because of lot size, frontage, coverage or floor-area ratio can be expanded as of right (no ZBA finding) if the addition meets current height, story and setback rules; and an unused nonconforming use keeps its status for four years instead of two.
questions: Which of these changes are already required by state law regardless of how Town Meeting votes, and which are local choices?
Roughly how many Medway homes sit on undersized or nonconforming lots and would gain as-of-right expansion?
articles.text: Amends Zoning Bylaw Section 5.5 (Nonconforming Uses and Structures) to conform to recent amendments to G.L. c. 40A. See the formatted redline for the full text.
articles.text_html:
Bold = new language  ·  Strikethrough = deleted language

To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 5.5 of the Zoning Bylaw, Nonconforming Uses and Structures, to conform to recent amendments to General Laws chapter 40A, as follows, new language shown in bold, deleted language shown in strikethrough:

1. Amend Section 5.5 Subsections A, B, and D as follows:

A. Applicability. Except as herein after provided, this Zoning Bylaw shall not apply to structures or uses lawfully in existence or lawfully begun, or to a building permit or special permit or other entitlement applied for under G.L. chapter 40A issued before the first publication of notice of the public hearing on this Zoning Bylaw or any amendments thereto, but shall apply to any change or substantial extension of such use, to a building permit or special permit issued after the first notice of said public hearing, to any reconstruction, extension or structural change of such structure and to any alteration of a structure begun after the first notice of said public hearing to provide for its use in a substantially different purpose or for the same purpose in a substantially different manner or to a substantially greater extent except where alteration, reconstruction, extension or a structural change to a one-family or two-family residential structure does not increase the nonconforming nature of said structure.

B. Commencement of Construction or Operation. Construction or operations under a building permit shall conform to any subsequent amendments to this Zoning Bylaw, unless the use or construction is commenced within a period of not more than twenty-four twelve months after the issuance of the last permit necessary for construction and, in any cases involving construction, unless such construction is continued through to completion as continuously and expeditiously as is reasonable. The twenty-four month period shall be tolled during any time the applicant is actively seeking or obtaining other necessary permits. Construction or operations under a special permit issued pursuant to G.L. c. 40A, §9 or site plan approval pursuant to this Zoning Bylaw shall conform to any subsequent amendments to this Zoning Bylaw or of any other local land use regulations unless the use or construction is commenced within a period of 3 years after the issuance of the special permit or site plan approval and, in cases involving construction, unless such construction is continued through to completion as continuously and expeditiously as is reasonable. For the purpose of the prior sentence, construction involving the redevelopment of previously disturbed land shall be deemed to have commenced upon substantial investment in site preparation or infrastructure construction, and construction of developments intended to proceed in phases shall proceed expeditiously, but not continuously, among phases.

D. Nonconforming Uses. Legally pre-existing nonconforming uses may be extended or altered, provided, that no such extension or alteration shall be permitted unless there is a finding by the Zoning Board of Appeals as the special permit granting authority that such extension or alteration shall not be substantially more detrimental than the existing nonconforming use or structure to the neighborhood. The Zoning Board of Appeals may grant a special permit to change or substantially extend a nonconforming use only if it determines that such change or extension shall not be substantially more detrimental than the existing nonconforming use to the neighborhood.

2. Add a new Section 5.5.F as follows, and re-lettering the remaining subsections accordingly:

F. Notwithstanding the above provisions, legally existing pre-existing nonconforming structures or residential uses that do not conform to zoning because of lot size or shape, frontage, lot coverage or floor area ratio requirements may be extended or altered as of right, without the need for a finding by the special permit granting authority under this paragraph, if such extension or alteration complies with the current dimensional regulations regarding height, stories, and setback.

3. Amend current Section 5.5.F, Abandonment or Non-use

G. Abandonment or Non-Use. Any nonconforming use that has been abandoned, or not used for more than two years, or more than four years effective July 1, 2026, shall lose any protected nonconforming status, and shall be subject to all of the provisions of this Zoning Bylaw.

Or act in any manner relating thereto.

articles.title: Raise and Appropriate: Debt Service and Assessors' Revaluation
articles.summary: Raises $1,040,000 on the tax levy: $1,000,000 to supplement the FY2027 debt service budget and $40,000 for the Assessors' revaluation account. The Finance Committee had not taken a position when the warrant was signed.
questions: What new or changed debt requires an extra $1M in FY27 debt service after the May budget was set?

articles.text: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate the sum of $1,040,000 with $1,000,000 therefrom to supplement the Fiscal Year 2027 debt service budget and $40,000 to supplement the Assessors' revaluation account, or act in any manner relating thereto.

tax_impact.tip: Rough estimate: $1.04M ÷ about $4.03B of taxable value (FY26 levy ÷ FY26 rate) ≈ $0.26 per $1,000 of assessed value. See Background for details and caveats.

background.html:
Rough estimate: Raising $1,040,000 on the tax levy works out to about $0.26 per $1,000 of assessed value, or about $26 for every $100,000 of a property's assessed value.

What that means for a typical home

  • $500,000 assessed value: about $129
  • $600,000: about $155
  • $700,000: about $181
  • $800,000: about $207

To estimate your own share, take your assessed value (shown on your tax bill), divide by 100,000, and multiply by $26.

How this was estimated

  • FY2026 tax levy: $56,364,170 (Finance Committee Report to the 2026 Annual Town Meeting).
  • FY2026 tax rate: $14.00 per $1,000. Medway uses a single rate for residential and commercial property (Assessing Department).
  • Implied total taxable value: $56,364,170 ÷ $14.00 × 1,000 ≈ $4.03 billion.
  • $1,040,000 ÷ $4.03 billion × 1,000 ≈ $0.26 per $1,000. That's about 1.8% of the FY2026 levy.
Caveats: This is a rough, illustrative figure, not a tax-bill projection. The FY2027 tax rate and property values have not been set yet. Whether bills actually go up by this amount depends on how much unused room the Town has under its Proposition 2½ levy limit and on the rest of the FY2027 tax-rate setting. The Finance Committee had not made a recommendation on this article when the warrant was signed.
Sources:
  • Medway Assessing Department (FY2026 tax rate) · historical tax rates (PDF)
  • Finance Committee Report to the 2026 Annual Town Meeting, Fiscal Year Summary (FY2026 property tax levy)
Estimate prepared with AI assistance from published Town figures. Check with the Assessing Department or Finance Director for authoritative numbers.
